ain

/'ain/
numberclasscardinalnumber
masc fem neut pl
nom ain aina ain ain
one
OHGeinOEānONeinnGothicains
Pwgc ain Daughter forms by century-ish: Gothic ains (Wulfila, 4th c.) — diphthong intact Old Norse einn (n-assimilation later) Old English ān — monophthongized Old Saxon ēn — monophthongized Old Frisian ēn / ān — monophthongized Old High German ein — diphthong preserved Wachtendonck ēin (9th–10th c. Ripuarian Frankish) — mixed/transitional spelling, the long ē showing the monophthongization wave reaching Ripuarian from the Ingvaeonic side, the residual -i- preserving the older diphthongal coloring. Exactly what you'd expect from Central Franconian sitting on the Low/High German hinge. Siegfried's window is ~420 AD. Wachtendonck is 400–500 years downstream. The monophthongization that produced ēin hadn't happened yet, or was barely beginning. The strongest contemporary anchor is Gothic ains — Wulfila's translation is mid-4th c., one generation before Siegfried, and a different branch of Germanic preserving the diphthong tells you the diphthong was the live form across the whole family in that window. OHG ein on the adjacent dialect continuum confirms it from the other side: High German never monophthongized this vowel at all, so its preservation there is the strongest signal that the diphthong was the original Frankish form before regional drift split things.

ain enti twaintig

/ain 'enti 'twaintiɣ/
numbernumber
twenty-one (one and twenty)
OHGein inti zweinzugOEān and twēntigONeinn ok tuttuguGothicains jah twai tigjus
Twenty-one. Composition pattern: [ones] + enti + [tens], ones-before-tens throughout the teens-to-nineties range above 20. Cf. Gothic fimf jah twai tigjus (Luke 9:14), OE fīf and twēntig, OHG fimf inti zweinzug, modern German fünfundzwanzig. The pattern is fully productive for 21-99: X enti Y-tig for any single-digit X and any decade Y-tig.

oath, solemn promise, sworn binding
OHGeidOEāþONeiðrGothicaiþs
used in
Ni sī aiþ, oƀ ni sī blōd.
There is no oath if there is no blood.
Aiþ ni skal man brekan.
An oath one shall not break.
Aiþbrōþre bindant aiþ mid blōde.
The oath-brothers bind the oath with blood.
PGmc *aiþaz. Diphthong *ai retained in 5th c. Ripuarian; monophthongization to ē happens later in coastal West Germanic dialects but not yet in Siegfried's speech.

/'aiθbroːθer/

oath-brother (sworn ritual brotherhood)
OHGeidbruoderOEāþbrōðorONeiðbróðir
used in
Þū bis mīn aiþbrōþer
You are my oath-brother.
Aiþbrōþre winnant
Oath-brothers strive (together).
Aiþbrōþre farant in rīne.
Oath-brothers travel in the Rhine.
Aiþbrōþre sāhun sigifriþ.
Oath-brothers saw Sigifriþ.
Werþe sigifriþ mīn aiþbrōþer.
May Sigifriþ become my oath-brother.
Ik weit þat sigifriþ ist aiþbrōþer mīn.
I know that Sigifrīþ is my oath-brother.
Þan sigifriþ nam swerd, sāhun aiþbrōþre.
When Sigifrīþ took the sword, the oath-brothers saw.
Sigifriþ, aiþbrōþer mīn, winnit gunþ.
Sigifrīþ, my oath-brother, wins the battle.
Aiþbrōþre bindant aiþ mid blōde.
The oath-brothers bind the oath with blood.
Compound of aiþ + brōþer. Refers to sworn ritual brotherhood, a real Germanic institution (Eidbruderschaft). Most strongly attested in ON eiðbróðir; OE āþbrōðor and OHG eidbruoder also occur. Declines on the second element following the brōþer r-stem paradigm.

arlausjan

/ar'lausjan/
verbclassClass 1 Weak
infarlōsjanimp sgarlōsiimp plarlōsiadpast ptcarlōsid
pres pres sbjv past past sbjv
1sg arlōsju arlōsje arlōsta arlōsti
2sg arlōsis arlōsjēs arlōstēs arlōstīs
3sg arlōsit arlōsje arlōsta arlōsti
1pl arlōsjamēs arlōsjēm arlōstum arlōstīm
2pl arlōsit arlōsjēt arlōstud arlōstīt
3pl arlōsjant arlōsjēn arlōstun arlōstīn
to set free
OHGirlōsen, arlōsenOEālīesanGothicuslausjan
used in
Endi ni farlaidjas uns in kostunga, ok arlōsi uns fan uƀile.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
Class 1 weak, prefixed. Chose ar- over ir-/er-: ar- is the northern preservation on the OS/OE isogloss; ir- is the OHG innovation from unstressed vowel raising; er- is the post-medieval MHG development. 5th c. Ripuarian sits pre-raising. PGmc *uz-lausijaną, causative to *leusaną "to lose"; PIE *leu- "to loosen". Past dental after voiceless -s- devoices to -st- (same phonotactic rule as wīhta < wīh+d-). Prefixed verb takes no ga- in past participle. Cognates: OS ālōsian (Heliand renders "libera nos a malo" with this verb), OE ālīesan, OHG irlōsen, Goth uslausjan. Semantic path: loosen/release from bondage > redeem — inherited from PIE, not a Christian-era calque.

singular
nomauga
genaugin

eye
OHGauga, ougaOEēageONaugaGothicaugō
used in
Sigifriþes augun sind blāo
Sigifriþ's eyes are blue.
PGmc *augō- "eye." Retains diphthong /au/ in 5th-c. Ripuarian because the following /g/ is velar, outside the dental-conditioned monophthongization environment. Parallels OHG auga (preserved diphthong). The later non-dental northern monophthongization (Old Saxon ōga, Old Low Franconian/Wachtendonck ōuga 9th-10th c., Middle Dutch oog) is post-Siegfried by 4+ centuries. Modern Kölsch Aug (sg.) / Ooge (pl.) preserves both reflexes within a single inflectional paradigm.

balder

/'balder/
namegendermascreligion/spiritual
singular
nombalder
genbalderes
datbaldere
accbalder
Balder (god)
OHGBalderOEBealdorONBaldr
used in
Þō warþ þemō Balderes folon sīn fōt biwrenkid.
Then Balder's foal's foot was wrenched.
The god Balder / Baldr. PGmc *Baldraz, from adjective *balþaz 'bold' + agent/nominal -raz. Cognates: ON Baldr (Æsir god, son of Óðinn), OHG Balder (attested in Merseburg Charm 2 as Balderes gen.sg), OE Bealdor (used as common noun 'prince, lord' in Beowulf, e.g. "sinca bealdor" prince-of-treasures — same word, semantic split). Etymological doublet with the common-noun sense preserved lexically as separable homophone in OE; in Ripuarian at Sigifrið's stage both may coexist. Ripuarian form Balder: preserved -er suffix, unshifted single d, no i-mutation (no -j- trigger). Genitive Balderes appears in Merseburg Charm 2 line 2 in possessor-dative-with-body-part construction.

Neuter a-stem. PGmc *braudą. Wachtendonck-style au > ō monophthongization applied; d retained (pre-consonant-shift Ripuarian, does not go to t as in later OHG). All WGmc/NGmc/Gothic descendants are neuter — OS brōd, OHG brōt, OE brēad, ON brauð, Goth brauþ (attested Mt 26:26). Gender in DB corrected from masc → neut. Semantic doublet with hlaif — OHG/OS/OD prefer this brōd root, OE and Gothic-primary use hlāf/hlaifs. Same branch-split shape as hailagōn (WGmc, from *hailag-) vs wīhjan (from *wīh-, closer to Goth weihs).

dagalīk

/'daɣaliːk/
adjectivetime
masc fem neut pl
nom dagalīk dagalīku dagalīk dagalīke
acc dagalīkan dagalīka dagalīka dagalīke
daily

used in
Brōd unser dagalīka giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Hlaiƀ unseran dagalīkan giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Adjective, "daily, of-this-day, pertaining-to-the-day." Formation: dag (root of dagaz, "day") + -e- linking vowel + -līk (productive WGmc adjective-forming suffix, from PGmc *-līkaz, cognate to English -ly, German -lich, from the noun *līką "body, form, likeness"). Full strong declension in OS/pre-shift Ripuarian style — nom sg: dagalīk/dagalīku/dagalīk (M/F/N), acc sg: dagalīkan/dagalīka/dagalīka (M/F/N with -a rather than OHG -az for neut), dat sg: dagalīkumu/dagalīkeru/dagalīkumu, nom pl: dagalīke/dagalīka/dagalīk. For Pater Noster line 3 modifying brōd (neut acc sg), the surface form is dagalīka (OS-style neut acc sg strong). Standard WGmc rendering of Vulgate ,,quotidianum,' itself a simplification of Greek ,,ἐπιούσιον' — a hapax legomenon that Jerome flagged as vocabulary he was inventing. Alternate root worth noting: OHG-St.Gall uses ,,emizzīg' (continual, incessant) from PGmc *ammatiga- for the same slot, a completely different lexical choice.

deutonburg

/'deutonburɣ/
namegenderneutplace name
Duisburg (on the Ruhr) (Literal: Fortress of Deuto)
OHGTusburch
Deutonburg means "fort of Deuto" or "fort of the people," and the ambiguity between those two readings does not need to be resolved. Deuto is a documented Germanic personal name; the root þeud- means "people" (the same root that gives modern Dutch and Deutsch); and the compound form Deuton- fits both readings equally well. Whichever it started as — an eponymous founder, a real person, or a bare descriptive stem — the surface form is identical. The Latin attestation Castrum Deutonis is the direct source of the Germanic reconstruction. The two forms are the same name in two languages. Latin uses castrum ("fort") followed by the possessor in genitive case (Deutonis, "of Deuto"). Germanic uses the possessor in compound-first position followed by burg ("fort"). This is a standard translation pattern — Latin fortification word out, Germanic burg in, name preserved. The same substitution shows up in dozens of Rhine and Danube place names that started as Roman castra and became German -burg cities. The transition from the historical Deut- to the modern Duis- witnesses the High German Consonant Shift operating in this territory. The medial -t- of Deut- shifted to -s-, giving Duis-, in the same sound change that turned water into Wasser and it into es further south. This matters because Duisburg sits above the Uerdingen line — the northernmost line marking the shift that scholars usually draw on the map. The place name is a frozen witness that the t→ss shift operated further north than the standard line admits, sitting alongside the "ss" pronunciation preserved in Xantener Platt and the "wasser" spelling in the Wachtendonck Psalms as three independent pieces of evidence pointing the same direction. The dating gets interesting. Saint Jerome, writing his Chronicon around 380 AD, mentions a place called Deuso in the region of the Franks — "apud Deusonem in regione Francorum" — in connection with a Roman campaign against the Saxons in 373 AD. The identification of Jerome's Deuso is contested: it may be Duisburg on the Ruhr, or Doesburg on the IJssel in modern Gelderland, or Deutz across the Rhine from Cologne. All three candidates sit north of the Uerdingen line, so the uncertainty does not affect the argument about the shift's northern reach. What is striking is that Jerome writes -s- in 380 AD, while later Latin sources for the Ruhr city write -t- (Castrum Deutonis). Read as linear evolution, that sequence runs backwards — the shift cannot happen and then un-happen. Read as two different transmission paths, it works. Jerome, working from a Roman military informant, wrote what the Franks actually said with the -s- already there. Later Latin chancery writing reached for a more classical-looking spelling by analogy with the Roman tribe name Teutones and restored a -t- that was not present in the local pronunciation. Deutonis is hypercorrection — Latin scribes writing what a name should look like in proper Latin — not evidence of when the shift happened. Modern Duisburg preserves the continuously-Germanic pronunciation from before Jerome through medieval times to today. Not to be confused with Dispargum. Gregory of Tours mentions Dispargum in his Historia Francorum (late 6th century) as an early Frankish royal seat, and the name occasionally gets swept together with Duisburg's etymology because of the superficial resemblance. The two are separate. Dispargum is generally identified with Duisburg-Tervuren, a site in modern Brabant near Leuven, not with the Ruhr city. The confusion is common but does not belong in the Ruhr-Duisburg reconstruction chain. Old Low Franconian: Diusburch

fargeƀan

/far'ɣeβan/
verbclassClass V Strong
inffargeƀanimp sgfargiƀimp plfargeƀadpast ptcfargeƀan
pres pres sbjv past past sbjv
1sg fargeƀu fargeƀe fargaƀ fargāƀi
2sg fargiƀis fargeƀēs fargāƀi fargāƀīs

to forgive, pardon; to give away, hand over
OHGfargebanOEforġiefanONfyrirgefaGothicfragiban
used in
Endi fargiƀ uns skuldi unsere, sō wē fargeƀamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Class V strong "give-away, for-give." Prefixed derivative of geƀan (id 335) — the far- prefix (PGmc *fra-, cognate with Latin pro-, Greek pro-) carries the semantics of separation/away-movement. Full ablaut series inherited from geƀan: e — a — ē — e. 2sg/3sg present show i-mutation (fargiƀis, fargiƀit) matching giƀis/giƀit. Past participle is fargeƀan (no gi- prefix since far- occupies the prefix slot). Imperative 2sg fargiƀ carries the i-mutation from the pres 2sg/3sg stem. Used in Lord's Prayer line 4 (Mt 6:12) as the fargeƀan-variant paired with farlātan-variant — two competing "forgive" verbs both attested in Germanic Bible tradition. Cognates: OHG fargeban/firgeban, OS fargeƀan, OE forġiefan, ON fyrirgefa, Goth fragiban.

farlaidjan

/far'laidjan/
verbclassClass 1 Weak
inffarlaidjanimp sgfarlaidiimp plfarlaidiadpast ptcfarlaidid

OHGfirleitenOEforlǣdan
used in
Endi ni farlaidjas uns in kostunga, ok arlōsi uns fan uƀile.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
Class 1 weak, prefixed (far- = moral-directional astray-prefix). PGmc *fra-laidijaną, causative of *līþaną "to go, travel" (ai = ablaut e-grade). Stem-final -d + weak past suffix -d- yields geminate -dd- (cf. OS farlēdde, OE forlǣdde). Prefixed verb takes no ga- in past participle. Cognates: OS farlēdian (Heliand, exact rendering of "inducere in tentationem"), OHG firleiten, OE forlǣdan. Chosen over ga-prefix because 5th c. Ripuarian preserves the ga-/far- semantic split productively (ga- = neutral completive, far- = moral/astray), pattern preserved north-Rhenish through Heliand and Wachtendonck; Tatian gileiten reflects southern collapse of this distinction under mechanical Latin-glossing.

fiuwer hund enti fimf enti twaintig

/'fiuwer hund 'enti fiɱf 'enti 'twaintiɣ/
numbernumber

OHGfior hunt inti fimf inti zweinzugOEfēower hund and fīf and twēntigONfjögur hundruð ok fimm ok tuttuguGothicfidwor hunda jah fimf jah twai tigjus
Four hundred and twenty-five (425). Three-digit composition pattern: [hundreds-count] + hund + enti + [ones-and-tens tail]. Only one enti binds the ones-and-tens pair; hundreds attach unmarked. Chosen as a demonstration number because 425 is the approximate date of the Bergakker inscription — the only directly attested 5th-century Frankish text in the corpus. For arbitrary Y hundred and X: [Y] hund enti [ones enti tens].

Þō warþ þemō Balderes folon sīn fōt biwrenkid.
Then Balder's foal's foot was wrenched.
Weak masculine n-stem noun "foal, young horse". PGmc *fulan-. Class-defining features: nom.sg -o (from PGmc *-ō), oblique stem in -in-/-en- (< *-in-) and -on-/-un- (< *-un-). Dat.sg folon matches Merseburg Charm 2 attestation (uolon), where the -on ending shows syncretism with acc.sg — a real feature of WGmc weak n-stem paradigms where dat.sg and acc.sg often collapse under the -on/-un shape. Compare willjo (id 1002) and skuldigo (id 1071) in the corpus, which take dat.sg -en; folo shows the variant -on. Both endings coexisted in WGmc; the -on form dominates in the Charm attestation and is set here as primary. Cognates: OHG folo (dat.sg folen ~ folon), OS folo, OE fola, ON foli. Ripuarian preserves initial f- unshifted and short -o- (no i-mutation, no diphthongization).

frisk

/'frisk/
adjectivequality
fresh
OHGfriscOEfersċONferskr
Found in Wartburg as "germanic". Form /frisk/ is the inherited Ripuarian reflex of PG friska- "fresh, new, unspoiled, vigorous, cool." Distinct evidentiary status: the Romance loan stratum (It. fresco, Sard. friscu, Cat. fresc, Sp./Pg. fresco, Friul. fresk, OFr. freis > Mod.Fr. frais) descends from a West Germanic borrowing into Vulgar Latin, NOT from Frankish specifically. Donor cannot be identified as Frankish vs. Old Saxon vs. general continental West Germanic because all dialects had /frisk/ with /sk/ preserved at the contact date and no diagnostic features distinguish them. Dating: 3rd-5th c. AD. Sardinian friscu may date the loan before Sardinian's split from continental VL (3rd-4th c.), possibly predating Frankish individuation as a distinct dialect (Franks first attested ~257 AD as Lower Rhine federation). OFr. freis shows /sk/ palatalization, dating loan into Gaulish VL before 5th-7th c. palatalization wave. Geographic distribution (present in Italian/Iberian/Gallo-Romance/Sardinian, absent in Romanian and Dalmatian) confirms western diffusion in late Imperial / post-Imperial period. Therefore: Romance reflexes are SIBLINGS of the Ripuarian form, not descendants, and confirm /sk/ preservation in West Germanic at the contact period without making Ripuarian the donor. PIE etymology uncertain; cf. Lith. prėskas "tasteless, unleavened," OCS prěsnъ "fresh, unleavened," possibly from PIE *preisk-, but vowel and -sk- suffix correspondences are not clean (Kroonen 2013 acknowledges Balto-Slavic comparanda without committing to a reconstruction).

fulla

/ˈfulla/
namegenderfemreligion/spiritual
singular
nomfulla
genfullūn
datfullūn
accfullūn
Fulla (goddess); the full one, the plentitude
OHGUolla, VollaONFulla
used in
Þō bigōl ina Frīja, Fulla ira swester.
Then Frīja sang [charms] over him, [and] Fulla her sister.
Goddess Fulla / Volla. PGmc *Fullō, fem. weak n-stem, from root *fullaz "full" — literally "the full one, the plentitude." Fertility/abundance figure. In this text, sister of Frīja and second in the healing-charm's female duo (Frīja / Fulla), parallel to Sunna / Sinthgunt. In Norse tradition (Snorra Edda) Fulla is Frigg's handmaiden who carries her casket and keeps her secrets. The Merseburg attestation confirms the sisters-of-goddesses pairing structure was pan-Germanic. Cognates: ON Fulla (weak n-stem, gen Fullu), OHG Uolla/Volla (Merseburg Charm 2 attestation with initial u-/v- for /f/, same convention as uuodan and uuorun which you already caught). Ripuarian: initial f- preserved unshifted, geminate -ll- from *-ll-, weak fem n-stem declension (nom -a, oblique -ūn). Cf. adjective *fullaz for etymological base.

Class VI Strong verb "to sing (magically), incant, chant". PGmc *galaną. Ablaut a—ō—ō—a matching faran/graƀan/dragan. The ritual-speech register verb: what the idisi and the healing goddesses do in the Merseburg Charms. Cognates: OHG galan, OS -galan (in compounds), OE galan "to sing, chant, enchant" (whence English "nightingale" < niht-galan "night-singer"), ON gala "to crow, chant". Prefix bi- (perfective/completive) gives bigōl "sang over, enchanted" as attested in Merseburg Charm 2 lines 3-5 ("thu biguol en X"). No separate bigalan headword needed — bi- rides on the surface form (same pattern as biwrenkid/wrenkjan in sentence 57).

galiþ

/ˈɡaliθ/
noungendermascbody part
singular
nomgaliþ
gengaliþes
datgaliþe
accgaliþ
instrgaliþu
plural
nomgaliþi
gengaliþō
datgaliþum
accgaliþi
joint, articulated limb, collection of limbs
OHGgilid
used in
Bain te baine, blōd te blōde, liþ te galiþum, sō sō galīmida sīn.
Bone to bone, blood to blood, limb to limbs, just so may they be joined.
Masculine u-stem noun "joint, collection of limbs, joined body-part". PGmc *ga-liþuz, formed on liþ (463, "limb, joint") with the ga- collective prefix that marks assemblage or aggregation. The prefix converts the individual limb-sense of liþ into the collective "joined-together limbs" sense — a body-part conceived as an articulated unit rather than a discrete member. Cognates: OHG gilid "joint, limb (collectively)", OS gelid, OD gilith. Not directly attested in Gothic as a compound (Gothic uses liþus in similar contexts without the ga- prefix) or ON (ON preserves the ga- as ø via prefix-loss, giving bare liðr). The two-way WGmc attestation (OHG + OS + OD) is sufficient reconstruction support given the transparent prefix morphology on an already-solid base. Ripuarian preserves ga- (unshifted from OHG gi-) and -þ- (unshifted from OHG -d-). Merseburg Charm 2 line 8 attests dat.pl as "geliden" — this reflects OHG *-þ- → -d- voicing/shift AND *-um → -en unstressed weakening. Ripuarian dat.pl galiþum preserves both features in their pre-OHG form. Paradigm inherits from liþ directly: u-stem masc with -i plural (galiþi, not -ōs), -um dat.pl, -u instrumental singular preserving the historical u-stem theme vowel.

Form /gilda/ "guild, sacrificial association" reconstructed for Ripuarian is uncertain. FEW gives the headword as anfrk. gilda but the geographic distribution of attested cognates (MDu ghilde, MLG gilde, OFris jelde, ON gildi) restricts the word's older usage to the North Sea Germanic region. OHG borrows the term from Low German only in the 17th century, suggesting it was not native to continental West Germanic. Old French gelde "band of foot soldiers" (Wace, Chrétien, 12th c.) likely traces to a Saxon, Frisian, or Low German donor rather than to Ripuarian specifically. Word retained in lexicon as POSSIBLE but not SECURELY reconstructible for 5th-century Ripuarian; the underlying verb /geldan/ "to pay" and noun /geld/ "payment" are secure, but the derived institutional feminine is not.

germja

/'ɣermia/
nounanimal
young ewe, lamb
Spelled as germia in Wartburg. Surface form: */germja/, feminine ja-stem (West Germanic productive feminine class with the -ja- thematic suffix). Gloss: "young ewe, ewe-lamb, female sheep not yet having borne offspring." Phonology against your locked frame: the /r/ here is the inherited PG */r/ (alveolar, not from rhotacism of */z/), so this is regular /r/ NOT your transitional ʐ/ʀ. The /m/ is stable. The /j/ is the West Germanic palatal glide forming the feminine ja-stem suffix. No phonological surprises. Cognates: directly attested only through the Romance loan stratum and the 9th-century medieval Latin orthography of the Polyptychon. No clear Germanic cognates in other branches with the same semantics — OHG, OE, ON, OS, OFris don't have a clear */germja-/ "ewe" word that you can point to. Proposed ON garmr "dog" is semantically distant and should be flagged as uncertain. This makes the word a "Frankish-isolate" or near-isolate within Germanic — defensible because the Polyptychon attestation is direct primary evidence of the word's existence in West Frankish territory in the 9th century, with the Old French reflexes confirming continuous Frankish use into the medieval period, but you can't triangulate cognates from sister Germanic languages because they didn't preserve the word.

OHGhaft, haptOEhæftONhaftrGothichafts (in cmpd)
used in
Suma hapt heftidun, suma hari lettidun, suma klūƀōdun umbi kōni-wiþi.
Some fastened fetters, some hindered the army, some picked at the war-fetters around.
Inspring hapt-bandum, andfar wīgandum.
Spring out from fetter-bonds, escape from warriors.
Neuter a-stem noun "fetter, bond, captivity". Substantivized past participle of *hafjan "to seize, capture" (cognate Lat. capio, related to Modern German Haft). Same etymological root as the adjective haft (1252) — the adjective is the participle "bound", the noun is "the state of being bound, the bond itself". OHG has both haft and hapt spellings; the -pt- variant preserved here as a philologically distinct headword to reflect Merseburg Charm 1 orthography. Cognates: OHG haft, OE hæft, OS haft, ON haftr, Goth. hafts (in compounds).

hiudag

/'hiudaɣ/
adverbtime
today
OHGhiutuOEhēodæġGothichimma daga
used in
Brōd unser dagalīka giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Hlaiƀ unseran dagalīkan giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Temporal adverb, indeclinable. From PGmc *hiu (demonstrative "this," the ja-stem instrumental of *hiz) + *dag- (root of *dagaz "day"). The fused adverb represents an early stage before the dative -u ending crystallized (later stage: hiudagu > hiudu > OHG hiutu > modern German heute). The unfused two-word ancestor is visible in Gothic ,,himma daga' (dat masc dem + dat sg dag). Ripuarian at 5th c. sits at the point where fusion is happening but before the case-ending erosion. Semantic scope: ,,today, on this day, this present day.' Direct temporal adverb, not a prepositional phrase.

/'xlaiβ/
noungendermascfood & drink

bread, loaf
OHGhleib, leibOEhlāfONhleifrGothichlaifs, hlaibs
used in
Hlaiƀ unseran dagalīkan giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Masculine a-stem. PGmc *hlaibaz. Intervocalic ƀ /β/ (bilabial fricative) is the pre-shift Ripuarian allophone of /b/ between vowels — same convention as geƀan. Semantic doublet with brōd (id 176) for "bread" — hlaiƀ is the Gothic/OE-lineage word (Goth hlaifs, OE hlāf), brōd is the OHG/OS/OD-lineage word (OHG brōt, OS brōd, Wachtendonck brōt). Both roots existed in Ripuarian and either could be used liturgically; the choice is a philological reconstruction call. Cognates: Goth hlaifs, OE hlāf, OHG hleib (with i-mutation), ON hleifr, Ripuarian hlaiƀ preserves the PGmc /ai/ diphthong.

/'hol/
noungenderneut
hollow, hole
OHGholOEholONholr
Can also be adjective. Wartburg FEW vol. XVI, p. 128 reconstructs Old Low Franconian *hal "cave" based solely on late Norman halot (1669) and disputed OE hāl "secret place." Brüch (ZrP 38:693) proposed; Gamillscheg countered with dissimilation from *holot. Wartburg refuses to call it. Excluded from lexicon. *hol used instead as the inherited form from PGmc *hulaz, with broad Germanic support (OHG/OS/OE hol, ON holr).

holt

/'holt/
noungenderneutnature
singular
nomholt
genholtas
datholta
accholt
instrholtu
plural
nomholtu

datholtum
accholtu
instrholtum
woods, forest, wood
OHGholzOEholtONholt
used in
Pol endi wōdan fōrun te holta.
Pol and Wōdan went to the wood.
Neuter a-stem noun 'wood, forest, grove'. Long-stem, heavy syllable (h-olt). Dat.sg holta preserves archaic ending -a (< PGmc *-ai) rather than the reduced -e found in most neuter a-stems in the corpus (baine, swerde, blōde, brōde). Retention likely reflects ritual/formulaic register — appears in Merseburg Charm 2 line 1 (Ripuarian: Pol endi wōdan fōrun te holta). Nom/acc.pl holtu follows the corpus convention for neuter a-stems regardless of stem weight (compare swerdu, blōdu, brōdu). Cognates: OHG holz (with t→z second sound shift), OS holt, OE holt, ON holt. Ripuarian preserves unshifted t.

hrōra

/'xroːra/
nameplace name
Ruhr
Not attested for the 5th century. Latin Rura is 8th century. Reconstruction from PGmc hrōr- (stir, movement) via folk etymology or genuine inheritance; the same root gives OHG ruora and the lexicon's own hrōrjan (id 1220). Whether Ruhr originated as a native Germanic hydronym or as a Germanicized substrate name in the Old European hydronymic layer, by the 5th century Frankish pronunciation would run through this form.

hund

/'hund/
numberclassneutnumber
hundred
OHGhuntOEhundONhundraðGothichund
Hundred. From PIE *ḱm̥tóm > PGmc *hunda- (neuter noun). Cf. Gothic hund, OE hund (later reinforced as hundred with -rǣd count-suffix), OHG hunt (post-shift), OS hund. Pre-shift Ripuarian keeps intact final -d and initial /x/ per locked convention. Homophonous with hund "dog" (id 319, PGmc *hundaz) — same phonological shape, unrelated etymology. Native speakers distinguish by context; the number takes numeral syntax, the animal takes noun syntax.

Our Father, Thou art in Heaven, Hallowed be Thy name.
Brōd unser dagalīka giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Hlaiƀ unseran dagalīkan giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Endi farlāt uns skuldi unsere, sō wē farlātamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Endi fargiƀ uns skuldi unsere, sō wē fargeƀamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Endi ni farlaidjas uns in kostunga, ok arlōsi uns fan uƀile.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
Ik willju sehan swerd, þat sigifriþ gaƀ.
I want to see the sword that Sigifrīþ gave.
Ik weit þat sigifriþ ist aiþbrōþer mīn.
I know that Sigifrīþ is my oath-brother.
Ēr þū feris, giƀ mē brōd.
Before you go, give me bread.
Sō sigifriþ ferit, sō ik faru.
As Sigifrīþ goes, so I go.
Sō þiodarīk winnit, sō winnamēs wē.
Just as Þiodarīk strives, so we strive.
Sigifriþ, aiþbrōþer mīn, winnit gunþ.
Sigifrīþ, my oath-brother, wins the battle.
Wurd ni mugun wē fliohan.
Fate we cannot flee.
PGmc *ek (1sg). Pre-High German consonant shift form: k retained (OHG ih shows the later k → x shift, post-Siegfried). Suppletive oblique forms from PGmc *m-. Cognates: Gothic ik, OS ik, OE ic, ON ek.

kostunga

/'kostunga/
noungenderfem
singular
nomkostunga
genkostungō
datkostungu
acckostunga
plural
nomkostungō
genkostungōno

temptation
OHGkostungaOEcostnunge
used in
Endi ni farlaidjas uns in kostunga, ok arlōsi uns fan uƀile.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
Feminine ō-stem, -ungō deverbal abstract noun subclass (like lôsunga id 428, hrunga id 308, tunga id 878). PGmc *kustungō, deverbal to *kustōną "to test, put on trial", denominative to *kustiz "choice, test"; PIE *ǵeus- "to taste, choose" (cf. Lat gustāre, Gk geúomai). Inherited stock, not a Christian-era coinage — the "temptation/trial" sense maps onto Latin tentātiō from parallel semantic paths ("put to the test"). Pan-West-Germanic distribution: OE costnung, OS kostunga (Heliand, temptation-verse), OHG kostunga (Tatian, Notker); Old Frisian gap likely attestation-only. Ripuarian sits geographically between OS and OHG witnesses, gets the form by inheritance from all three neighbors. Form without -n- (kostunga not kostnunga) follows the continental Frankish trend (OHG/OS); the -n- of OE costnung is an insular preservation of the verbal present stem. Used accusative singular after "in" for directional-into (Latin "in tentationem" parallel).

krabbōn

/'krabːoːn/
verbclassClass 2 Weak
to crab, scratch, scrape, claw at
Wartburg FEW vol. XVI, p. 349 reconstructs OLF *krabbatjan as a frequentative/intensive derivation built on the -atjan suffix, but he explicitly notes the form is "nicht belegt und auch nicht in spätern formen im germ. vertreten" — not attested in any Germanic source and not preserved in any later Germanic descendant. His reconstruction rests entirely on (a) the existence of MDu krabben as a base verb and (b) general morphological plausibility for the -atjan derivation; the Romance reflexes (Anjou/Poitou: crabacier, crabasser, etc.) show heavy analogical reshaping by passer, baller, and crépi. Geographic distribution (Anjou/Poitou) lies outside the Frankish substrate heartland. Wartburg's *krabbatjan-specific derivation is treated as speculative and excluded from this lexicon. Base verb *krabbôn used instead, with broad West Germanic cognate support (MDu/Dutch krabben, MLG krabben, modern German krabbeln, English crab, ON krafla). Written as krabbôn

kunnan

/'kunːan/
verbclassPreterite-Presentquality
infkunnanpast ptcgakund
pres pres sbjv past past sbjv
1sg kann kunni konda kondi
2sg kanst kunnīs kondēs kondīs
3sg kann kunni konda kondi
1pl kunnum kunnīm kondum kondīm
2pl kunnud kunnīt kondud kondīt
3pl kunnun kunnīn kondun kondīn
to know, recognize; can, to be able to
OHGkunnanOEcunnanONkunnaGothickunnan
used in
Þō bigōl ina Wōdan, sō hē wela konda.
Then Wōdan sang [charms] over him, as well he knew how.
Preterite-Present verb "to know (how), be able, understand". PGmc *kunnaną. Class III ablaut in present (u→a in sg, u in pl); weak past on *kunþ- > kund- stem. Meaning cluster covers cognitive knowledge (know a fact), practical skill (know how to), and modal ability (can, be able). The Charm 2 attestation "so he uuola conda" = "as well he knew how" uses the modal sense for Wōdan's ritual competence. Cognates: Gothic kunnan/kunþa, OS kunnan/konsta, OHG kunnan/konda~konsta, OE cunnan/cūþe (whence English "can/could" and "cunning"), ON kunna/kunna. Ripuarian preserves -nd- from PGmc *-nþ- (WGmc voicing), predating the OS/OHG -st- innovation. No imperative — preterite-present verbs are stative and lack imperative forms across Germanic.

kâda

/'kaːda/
noungenderfemfood & drink
singular
nomkâda
plural
nomkâdon, kâdun
Crackling, residue from rendered fat, leftover chunk from cooking
Pre-8th-century anfrk. borrowing per Frings (cited in Wartburg FEW XVI:293). Phonological diagnostics: initial k- preserved (not affricated to ch-, which would indicate later contact), intervocalic -d- preserved (not lenited). Reconstructed feminine ō-stem *kâda based on consistent feminine gender in modern Lower Rhenish and Dutch kade. Romance masculine reflexes (chaon, chon) derive from reanalysis of the anfrk. plural *kâdun/*kâdon as a singular -on noun during the Gallo-Romance contact period. Direct modern continuation: Lower Rhenish kade (rhein.) — Ripuarian target zone, no asterisk needed at the cognate level. Modern dialect restriction to Lower Franconian / Lower Rhenish is geographic contraction; original Frankish-period distribution covered all of Northern France (Wartburg note 2). See Rheinisches Wörterbuch 4:22 for modern distribution map.

kûla

/'kuːla/
noungenderfem
grave pit, dug hole
OHGkūlaONkúla
Wartburg FEW vol. XVI, p. 430 reconstructs OLF *kulister "burial site, gravesite" from MDu kûle "grave" + locative suffix -ster, citing as evidence only two Burgundian toponyms (Culêtre × 2 in Bourgogne). The compound *kulister is geographically Burgundian-only — no Lower Frankish reflexes, no Walloon-Picard-Lorrainian distribution, no Lower Rhenish toponymic continuation. Excluded from this lexicon as Burgundian-area Frankish, not Lower Rhenish / Ripuarian. The base noun *kûla "grave-pit, hollow in the ground" is independently recoverable from broad Lower Germanic cognate evidence (MDu kûle, modern Dutch kuil, modern German Kuhle, with funerary sense preserved in compound Grabkuhle) and is included here as a Ripuarian-relevant base form. Extract-the-base methodology pattern, same approach as *krabbôn from speculative *krabbatjan (FEW XVI:349).

liþ

/'liθ/
noungendermascbody part
singular
nomliþ
genliþes
datliþe
accliþ
instrliþu
plural
nomliþi
genliþō
datliþum
accliþi
bend, joint, body part, limb, member
OHGlidOEliþONliðrGothicliþus
used in
Sō sō bain-wrenki, sō sō blōd-wrenki, sō sō liþi-wrenki.
Just as bone-wrench, just as blood-wrench, just as limb-wrench.
Bain te baine, blōd te blōde, liþ te galiþum, sō sō galīmida sīn.
Bone to bone, blood to blood, limb to limbs, just so may they be joined.
Masculine u-stem "limb, joint, member (of body)". PGmc *liþuz (masc u-stem). Cognates: Gothic liþus (masc u-stem), ON liðr (masc u-stem, gen liðar), OS lith, OHG lid (later reanalyzed as neut a-stem in most attestations), OE liþ (neut, historically u-stem). Ripuarian preserves the u-stem heritage (masc, plural in -i not -ōs) matching Gothic and ON. The nom_sg/acc_sg have undergone -u loss (liþ, not liþu), giving a-stem-like singular but retaining u-stem plural morphology (liþi, not liþōs) — this is the same intermediate stage attested in OS lith, before the full OHG reanalysis to neut a-stem. Instrumental sg liþu preserves the historical u-stem vowel in a fossilized case. Compound-first-element form takes linking vowel -i- (as in liþi-wrenki, sentence 61) reflecting u-stem vestigial stem-vowel weakened, or analogical spread of i-stem compound patterns — this is a compositional form, not a paradigm cell. Initial þ preserved unshifted (Ripuarian pre-OHG feature; OHG shifts to lid/liden).

prottjan

/'protːjan/
verbclassClass 1 Weakspeech
to talk informally, to talk boastly, to babble
Class 1 weak verb (-jan class), reconstructed for 5th-century Xanten from the following evidence base and reasoning. The reconstruction rests primarily on phonological hard-lock evidence from dated German pfrassen, secondarily on cognate distribution across the northwestern Germanic branches, and is anchored geographically by the living Xantener reflex proot. The pfrassen evidence is the pivotal piece and dates the reconstruction unambiguously. Dated / obsolete German pfrassen shows both stages of the High German Consonant Shift applied to a form derived from *prattjan: word-initial p → pf (HGCS stage 1), and geminate tt → zz → later ss (HGCS stage 2). Full phonological derivation: *prattjan (class 1 weak, WGmc gemination applied) → *pfrattjan → *pfrazzjan → OHG pfrazzen → later German pfrassen. Every phonological rule that operated on native OHG vocabulary operated on this verb. This requires that the verb was present in the Continental West Germanic ancestor before HGCS began (c. 500 AD, initial stages substantially complete by c. 650 AD). A post-HGCS borrowing is ruled out — those would enter with unshifted p- and -tt-. The 5th-century Xanten reconstruction is therefore not merely defensible but required by the phonological evidence. The dated / obsolete status of pfrassen in modern German reflects later register displacement by sprechen inside High German after HGCS had already operated; the word existed long enough to be shifted, then lost the register competition in that branch. In the northern non-HGCS dialects (Low German, Low Franconian, Kleverländisch), the verb never underwent shift and survived in the register beneath sprekan without being displaced. Class 1 weak status is confirmed by Middle Dutch, which retains class 1 conjugation with the -tt- pattern in preterite forms. The mechanism producing the geminate: PGmc *pratjan / *protjan → WGmc gemination (t + j → tt) → *prattjan / *prottjan surface form → daughter reflexes. The geminate -tt- in OE prætt (noun, attested 9th–10th century) supplies the primary independent evidence for -jan origin: the gemination is not from any native geminate PGmc root but from the WGmc rule operating on the -jan suffix. Class shift from 1 to 2 (-ōn conjugation) happens in later daughters; modern Dutch praten (pret. pratede, pp. gepraat) is the endpoint of that shift, not the original conjugation. At 5th-century Xanten the verb sits firmly in class 1: infinitive *prottjan, present 1sg *prottju, present 3sg *prottiþ, preterite 3sg *prottida, past participle *ga-prottid. This is the paradigm to build the entry from. Attestation of the verb form in writing is late. No OHG attestation exists (the corresponding OHG form went through HGCS to pfrazzen / pfrassen but was already being displaced by sprechen). No Old Dutch or Old Low Franconian attestation exists — not in Wachtendonck, not in Corpus-Gysseling / VMNW. The earliest written attestation of the verb is c. 1440 in Middle Dutch praten "to chatter, speak informally," appearing in Palladius' De Re Rustica translation — an agricultural instruction manual, which is philologically diagnostic and discussed below. Middle Low German attests both praten and proten in the same 15th-century window. The related noun is attested substantially earlier: Old English prætt "trick, cunning, artful device, wile," from the 9th–10th century onward, is the earliest secure Germanic reflex of the root. Cognate distribution is restricted to the northwestern Germanic branches — Anglo-Frisian and Low Franconian / Low German — with a total gap in Old High German (except for the HGCS-shifted and later obsolete pfrassen) and in East Germanic (Gothic). Reflexes: OE prætt (9th–10th c.), ME praten (c. 1440), Modern English prate / prattle / prat; MDu praten (c. 1440); MLG praten and proten (15th c.); Modern Dutch praten; Modern Low German proten / proaten; Kleverländisch and Xantener Platt proot ("Ek proot platt" — living Xantener attestation); Saterland Frisian prat; dated German pfrassen (HGCS-shifted, obsolete); Norwegian prate, Swedish prata, Danish prate, Faroese práta, Icelandic prata (all borrowed from MLG per standard etymology, not independent Scandinavian survivals). The combination of complete absence from surviving OHG texts and presence of the HGCS-shifted pfrassen shows the word was in Continental West Germanic pre-HGCS and got squeezed out of the surviving written High German record by later displacement. Vowel uncertainty is real. OE prætt shows -a- with i-umlaut to æ (or possibly original -e-). MDu praten shows -a- without umlaut (Low Franconian resists i-umlaut more than Anglo-Frisian). MLG attests both praten and proten inside the same branch — the diagnostic that vowel variation was already present in early WGmc or was inherited from the substrate source with variant forms. dated German pfrassen shows -a-, matching the *prattjan variant. Modern LG continues the -o- variant (proten / proaten). Modern Xantener continues the -o- variant (proot). Since Xanten is the target dialect, *protjan is the local reconstruction, with *pratjan as the parallel Low Franconian / Dutch / HGCS-input form. The -o- is not a later shift or copyist's confusion; it is the northwestern-Rhineland / Low German branch reflex that Xanten's direct descendants preserve. Both vowel variants coexisted at the substrate borrowing stage. The PIE reconstruction *bred- "to wander, rove" proposed by Wiktionary and some older etymological sources is rejected. It rests on evidence from Germanic (praten / prettu- reflexes) and Balto-Slavic (Polish bredzić "to rave, jabber," Latvian bradāt "to talk nonsense") only. No reflexes exist in Celtic, Italic, Greek, Indo-Iranian, Anatolian, or Tocharian. Reconstruction of a PIE root from evidence in only two adjacent northern branches is not licensed by the comparative method. Every attested reflex sits inside a contiguous zone across the North European Plain, from the Netherlands eastward to the Baltic, with no southern IE branch attestation. This is the standard signature of shared Northern European substrate: pre-IE vocabulary borrowed independently into Germanic during its ethnogenesis in the northern zone and into Balto-Slavic during its formation to the east, both from a common substratum that predates both language families. The pattern is recognized in the substrate literature (Kortlandt, Kroonen 2013, Schrijver 2014, Boutkan) and has an established name: Northern European substrate, sometimes "Old European vocabulary" in older sources. The apparent shared root is not shared PIE inheritance but shared substrate borrowing at two different points. The correct etymology for *prottjan is: no PIE root, Nordwestblock substrate origin, with the broader Germanic + Balto-Slavic cognate distribution reflecting the wider Northern European substrate zone of which Nordwestblock is the western portion. Origin: Nordwestblock substrate. The Nordwestblock zone as defined by Kuhn 1959 (Vor- und frühgermanische Ortsnamen in Norddeutschland und den Niederlanden, ZfdA) runs from the Aller in the east to the Somme in the west, north of the Celtic-speaking zone, west of the Germanic core. Xanten sits inside the zone, near its northeastern edge. Kuhn's diagnostic features: p-initial vocabulary where Germanic morphology cannot produce it natively (PIE *b was extremely rare, Grimm's Law makes native p- words nearly impossible, so a Germanic p- word without a Latin loan explanation is a substrate candidate by default); toponyms in -apa (river), -loo (forest / clearing), -drecht (crossing / ford), -mar (bounded water), clustering densely in the zone and thinning sharply outside; vocabulary domains in agriculture, water, terrain, and everyday practice; lexical distribution restricted to the northwestern Germanic branches. *prottjan hits every diagnostic. Kuhn's original position (1959) allowed that the substrate language might have been an unknown IE branch, possibly Venetic-adjacent or a lost centum branch. Schrijver 2014 (Language Contact and the Origins of the Germanic Languages) argues the more radical position that large parts of the northwestern substrate were non-IE, with possible contact into a Finnic-adjacent or wholly isolated linguistic zone predating IE arrival in the North European Plain. Kortlandt and Boutkan have argued similar non-IE positions. Kroonen 2013 (Etymological Dictionary of Proto-Germanic) marks many northwestern-restricted p-words as substrate candidates explicitly. Boutkan's Old Frisian Etymological Dictionary is more aggressive still in labeling this stratum. Vennemann's Vasconic hypothesis is more radical and largely not accepted, but operates on the same register-preservation mechanism. Current consensus: Nordwestblock as a substrate zone is accepted; the exact nature of the substrate language(s) is contested; but the existence of significant non-Germanic (whether non-IE or a lost IE branch) substrate contributing vocabulary to the northwestern Germanic branches is mainstream, not fringe. Sociolinguistic register argument. Substrate vocabulary in every documented case survives preferentially in specific registers: agricultural terminology, local terrain vocabulary, traditional crafts, everyday informal speech, weather and seasons, emotional and expressive language. It disappears from ritual and religious language, warfare and nobility vocabulary, legal terminology, and written formal registers — all elite-controlled and connected to the incoming prestige culture. This is standard in the substrate literature (Schrijver 2014, Kortlandt, Boutkan). *prottjan / proten sits in the "informal speech act" register — exactly where substrate verbs preferentially survive. It coexists with sprekan (pan-Germanic, elite-carried, formal) not by competing but by holding a different register beneath it. The two verbs are not synonyms in social function even when they translate identically to Modern English "to speak." In High German, sprechen eventually displaced pfrassen and swallowed both registers; in the northern non-HGCS branches, the two verbs held their separate registers and both survived. Attestation gap explanation. The gap between OE prætt (9th–10th c.) and MDu praten (c. 1440) is not evidence against the verb's existence in the intervening centuries — pfrassen already proves the verb existed pre-6th century — but evidence of the sociolinguistic register the verb inhabited. Monastic Latin translation glosses did not need a word for everyday informal chatter; they needed sprekan-type verbs for "speak the Word." Charter and legal texts did not use commoner speech vocabulary. Courtly literature used elevated register. Runestones and heroic inscriptions used martial and elite forms. The word lived in oral commoner speech for centuries, invisible to the scribal record, until the specific text-type that needed it (agricultural instruction, Palladius 1440) finally appeared. The gap is a fingerprint of the word's sociolinguistic history, not evidence against continuity. The choice of Palladius' De Re Rustica for first attestation is philologically diagnostic: agricultural instruction cannot be delivered in elevated Latinate register and must use the words the actual farmers use. Population-genetics support for the substrate identification. Haak et al. 2015 established the Steppe / Yamnaya arrival at c. 2800 BC and the ancestry stratification it created across northern Europe. Olalde et al. 2018 on Bell Beaker (from c. 2500 BC) showed the elite-replacement model with variable completeness by region: near-total in Britain, more partial on the continent, especially in the northwestern coastal zone. Antonio et al. 2019 and subsequent work on continental European medieval samples show ongoing class-linked stratification. Y-chromosome R1a and R1b (Steppe markers) concentrate in elite lineages; older European mitochondrial haplogroups (U5, some H, some K) preserve at higher frequencies in the general population. For the Nordwestblock zone specifically, retention of Neolithic Farmer (EEF) ancestry runs measurably higher than in Central European populations; the Netherlands and northwestern German coastal populations sit at the high end of EEF component percentages across continental European samples. This is the demographic where substrate vocabulary would preferentially survive — descendants of the pre-IE speakers who named the local rivers and forests before Germanic speakers arrived. Cultural continuity compounds the genetic pattern: the commoner farming population inherited agricultural techniques adapted to the specific microclimates and soils of the Rhine delta and lowlands, and kept the vocabulary tied to that transmitted knowledge. Steppe-derived elites did not teach farming to the locals; they took political control over an existing agricultural society, and the vocabulary of that society is what became substrate. Methodological note. This entry is included on Xanten-anchored geographic-descent methodology, not on Proto-West-Germanic reconstructibility. The evidence hierarchy for a Xanten headword runs: Kleverländisch / Xantener living reflex → Middle Dutch and Middle Low German attestation → Old English northwestern-branch cognate → PWGmc plausibility check → OHG only where the southern development happens to preserve something the northwestern branch lost. HGCS-shifted evidence (pfrassen) counts as OHG-track confirmation of pre-6th century presence even where the surviving OHG textual corpus lacks the word. OHG textual absence is expected for a Nordwestblock substrate verb held in commoner register; the HGCS shift itself is the surviving trace. Requiring positive OHG textual attestation for a Xanten headword would be a methodological error equivalent to requiring French attestation to reconstruct a Portuguese word. Different branches. The correct reference frame for Xanten is the northwestern branch, with the phonological evidence of southern shifts providing dating anchors rather than reference forms. Source class: substrate / Nordwestblock. Not the same class as "reconstructed" (which implies PWGmc-derivable via comparative method from clean IE evidence) and not the same class as "Wartburg + Reconstructed" (which implies Frankish-substrate-in-Romance-based reconstruction). This entry represents a distinct source stratum: pre-Germanic Northern European substrate vocabulary held in commoner register through the entire history of the northwestern Germanic branches, phonologically datable to pre-6th century Continental West Germanic via HGCS-shifted German pfrassen, first entering the written record in 15th-century agricultural instruction texts, preserved directly in modern Xantener speech, geographically continuous with the pre-IE substrate zone from which it was originally borrowed. Broader cognate distribution across Germanic + Balto-Slavic without southern IE reflexes places it in the wider Northern European substrate zone of which Nordwestblock is the western portion. Register implications for Sigifrið. Þiðrekssaga has him raised outside pure court context — fostered by a smith (Mímir / Regin depending on manuscript tradition), spending formative time in forge and forest, then moving into courtly life at Worms. He would have grown up hearing and using both registers of the Xanten dialect. sprekan in oath-giving, council, court, ritual speech — pan-Germanic elite verb, appropriate for interaction with Frankish nobility, foreign courts, and formal ceremonial contexts. *prottjan (later proten, modern proot) with the smith, with the warband, with the commoners at Xanten, in ordinary conversation — Nordwestblock substrate verb his farming and craft neighbors used, appropriate for interaction with the population descended from the pre-IE substrate speakers whose land it still was in every sense that mattered outside the political frame. The verb selection is a sociolinguistic register-marker: it encodes who he is speaking to and how he positions himself in the moment. When he leaves Xanten and speaks at Gunther's court in Worms, he shifts toward sprekan. When he is back in the forge, back with his people, back at home, he shifts toward *prottjan. The distinction is character-relevant, not decorative.

Class V strong. PGmc *sehwaną. Verner alternation historically: past sg *sah (voiceless), past pl *sēgun (voiced, from Grammatischer Wechsel). OHG and OS levelled to uniform h (sāhum, sāhun); ON preserves g (sá / sá(g)um). Filled with the uniform-h pattern matching the West Germanic tradition. Cognates: OS sehan, OHG sehan, OE sēon, Goth saihwan.

debtor, guilty one
OHGsculdīgo, sculdīgerOEscyldiga, scyldigONskuldigrGothicskula, faihuskula
used in
Endi farlāt uns skuldi unsere, sō wē farlātamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Endi fargiƀ uns skuldi unsere, sō wē fargeƀamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Weak masculine n-stem "one who has skuld, debtor, guilty one." Formation: skuld (id 1069) + adjective suffix -ig ("having skuld, indebted, guilty") → substantivized as skuldigo (weak n-stem). This preserves the etymological pairing with skuld — the debita/debitoribus root identity of the Vulgate Lord's Prayer Mt 6:12 maps directly onto skuldi/skuldigom in Ripuarian. Weak declension follows the standard WGmc n-stem pattern: nom.sg -o, gen/dat.sg -en, acc.sg -on, nom/acc.pl -on, gen.pl -ōno, dat.pl -om. Cognates: OHG sculdīgo (with the -īgo agentive), OE scyldig/scyldiga, ON skuldigr, Goth skula (from the same PGmc *skula- root but formed as bare weak masc without -ig suffix). Related to skuld (1069) and to farlātan (985) / fargeƀan (1070) in the Pater Noster line 4 couplet.

swimman

/'swimːan/
verbclassClass III Strongmotion
infswimmanimp sgswimimp plswimmadpast ptcswommen
pres pres sbjv past past sbjv
1sg swimmu swimme swam swummi

Āl swimmit in rīne
The eel swims in the Rhine.
PGmc *swimmaną. Strong verb class III, nasal+consonant subtype. Infinitive identical across OE, OD, OHG (all swimman). Ablaut series i-a-u-o: present stem i (swimmit), past sg a-grade (swam), past pl u-grade (swummun), past participle o-grade (swommen). The past 2sg uses the plural u-grade stem (swummi) — class III peculiarity. Present plural endings use -amēs/-at/-ant rather than later OHG -emēs/-et/-ent.

sīn

/siːn/
pronounclasspossessivegrammar fundamentals
singular
nomsīn
gensīnes
datsīnemō
accsīnan
plural
nomsīne
gensīnerō
datsīnēm
accsīne
his, its (possessive adjective)
OHGsīnOEsīnONsinnGothicseins
used in
Þō warþ þemō Balderes folon sīn fōt biwrenkid.
Then Balder's foal's foot was wrenched.
Possessive adjective 'his, its' (3sg masc/neut anaphoric or reflexive). PGmc *sīnaz, from IE reflexive *swe- + adjectival suffix *-no-. Declines strong-adjective-style, agreeing with the possessed noun in case/number/gender — NOT with the possessor. Distinct grammatical category from the personal pronoun genitive es (gen.sg of hē, id 1171): sīn is attributive and inflects for the head noun; es is substantival/partitive and remains uninflected. Both categories coexist in Ripuarian and all early WGmc. The paradigm cells listed here give the strong-adjective masc/neut singular forms directly (the Charm 2 line 2 attestation "sīn uuoz" is nom.sg.masc agreeing with fōt); feminine and plural forms follow the standard strong-adjective pattern noted parenthetically in cell comments. No separate fem-possessive lexeme — feminine "her" uses ira (gen.sg of siu, id 1172) or the fem form of ira- (personal pronoun genitive extended into attributive use). Cognates: OHG sīn, OS sīn, OE sīn (poetic/archaic; largely replaced by his in prose), ON sinn, Goth. seins. Ripuarian preserves long ī unshifted.

unser

/'unser/
possessivegrammar fundamentals
masc fem neut pl
nom unser unseru unser unsere
acc unseran unsera unser unsere
our
OHGunsērOEūser, ūre, usserONvárr, órrGothicunsar
used in
Brōd unser dagalīka giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Hlaiƀ unseran dagalīkan giƀ uns hiudag
Give us this day our daily bread.
Endi farlāt uns skuldi unsere, sō wē farlātamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Endi fargiƀ uns skuldi unsere, sō wē fargeƀamēs skuldigom unserom.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
First-person plural possessive determiner. Declines like a strong adjective — nom sg endings -Ø/-u/-Ø/-e (M/F/N/pl), acc sg endings -an/-a/-Ø/-e. Historically the possessive stem derives from the genitive plural of the 1pl pronoun (PGmc *unser- from *ns-er-, gen pl of *wiz "we"), which then acquired adjectival inflection to agree with the possessed noun. In sentence 15 (Fader unser) the modifier appears as bare masc nom sg (unser modifies fader in nominative address). In sentence 28 (Brōd unser dagalīka) it appears as neut acc sg (also unser, homophonous with masc nom). In sentence 29 (Hlaiƀ unseran dagalīkan) it appears as masc acc sg (unseran, distinct from nom). Related to ik (id 45) — the gen pl form of ik also surfaces as "unser" (see sentence 15 pos 2 which uses the ik-collapse convention rather than pointing here). Future sentences pointing at possessive contexts should target this entry (1068) rather than ik (45). Cognates: OS ûsa/unsa, OHG unsēr, OE ūser/ūre, Goth unsar. All descend from PGmc *unser-.

3pl uƀarfarant uƀarfarēn uƀarfōrun uƀarfōrīn
to cross, cross over, traverse
OHGubarfaranOEoferfaranONyfirfara
used in
Þeuda uƀarfōr gafruranan Rīn.
The people crossed the frozen Rhine.
Þeuda uƀarfōr Rīn, þe fraus.
The people crossed the Rhine, which had frozen.
Prefix formation: uƀar- (preposition id 1457) + faran (id 182). Class VI strong, inherits faran's ablaut a — ō — ō — a and 2sg/3sg present i-mutation (uƀarferis, uƀarferit). Calque of Latin trānsīre, matching the OHG ubarfaran and OE oferfaran formations exactly. Compare infaran (id 1265) as a parallel prefixed derivation of faran with the same paradigm shape. Past participle is uƀarfaran without ga- prefix, standard for already-prefixed verbs (matching infaran > infaran, not *gainfaran).

wairda

/'wairda/
noungendermasc
woad, dye
OHGweitOEwādGothicwaisds
Written as waizda. Marked as "germ". Not Gothic. The Gothic hypothesis fails on geographic grounds. Gothic loans enter Gallo-Romance through the southern contact zone — the Visigothic kingdom in Aquitaine and the Iberian Peninsula — and surface in Occitan, Catalan, and Spanish. The reflexes of *waizda- show the opposite distribution. The earliest and densest attestations cluster in the northern Gallo-Romance belt: Picard waisde (1036, the earliest dated form on the page), waide; Wallonian wedde (Roisin); Flemish wouedde, wedde; Anglo-Norman wai(s)de. This is the heart of the Frankish settlement zone and the medieval Picard-Flemish dye economy. The central and southern French forms (guesde, gueide, guède) are downstream of northern donation — they reflect the regular /w-/ → /gw-/ → /g-/ treatment that affected Frankish loans as they propagated south through Gallo-Romance, not independent southern borrowing from Gothic. A Gothic donor would predict early Occitan and Iberian attestations and weak penetration into Picard-Wallonian; the actual distribution is the inverse. The donor population is Frankish, operating in the northern textile-dye economy where woad cultivation was concentrated.

PGmc *winnaną. Strong verb class III, nasal+consonant subtype. Infinitive identical across OE, OD, OHG (all winnan). Ablaut series i-a-u-u: present stem i (winnit), past sg a-grade (wann), past pl u-grade (wunnun), past participle u-grade (wunnen — geminate nn blocks lowering to o, unlike swommen). Original meaning is strive/struggle/toil/labor-for; the English semantic shift to "win" (achieve victory) is a late Old English development. Gothic winnan attests the related sense of "suffer" (cf. Gothic wunns "passion").

used in
Þō warþ þemō Balderes folon sīn fōt biwrenkid.
Then Balder's foal's foot was wrenched.
Sō sō bain-wrenki, sō sō blōd-wrenki, sō sō liþi-wrenki.
Just as bone-wrench, just as blood-wrench, just as limb-wrench.
Class 1 Weak jan-verb "to wrench, twist, sprain, dislocate". PGmc *wrankijan, causative-factitive built on the root *wrank- "twist, crooked" (adjective *wrangaz, whence English wrong). The -j- causative trigger yields i-mutation of the root vowel a → e throughout the paradigm (wrenk- not wrank-), and gemination is blocked because the root ends in -nk- (WGmc gemination applies only to single consonants). Initial wr- preserved in Ripuarian; OHG loses w- before r- word-initially (giving OHG renken), so this is a diagnostic pre-OHG feature. Prefix use: appears with bi- (completive/perfective) in the Merseburg Charm 2 attestation biwrenkid "wrenched" (past participle in the passive periphrasis with warþ). No separate biwrenkjan headword needed — bi- rides on the surface form and the participle links to this headword, same pattern as inspring/springan (sentence 55) and andfar/faran. Cognates: OHG renken (with w-loss), OE wrencan "to twist, deceive", MHG renken, MoG (ver)renken.

OHGwīgantOEwīgendONvígandiGothicweihands
used in
Inspring hapt-bandum, andfar wīgandum.
Spring out from fetter-bonds, escape from warriors.
Masculine nd-stem noun "warrior, fighter, combatant". Substantivized present participle of wīgan (1263) "to fight". Formation: verb stem wīg- + participial suffix -and- (PGmc *-and-, the same suffix that gives English present participles in -ing/-end). Parallel formations already in the dictionary: fīand (171) "enemy" < *fījan "to hate"; hailjand (1184) "savior" < *hailjan "to heal"; elpand (1231) "elephant" (etymologically the same nd-stem, from OHG helfant "helper" reanalyzed as an animal name). Cognates: OHG wīgant, OS wīgand, OE wīgend "warrior" (Beowulf and other heroic poetry), ON vígandi, Goth. weihands (participle). Attested in Merseburg Charm 1 line 5 (vigandun = dat pl). Dat pl form: wīgandum (matches Merseburg vigandun with pre-weakening -um). Semantic range: "one who fights" in the heroic register — a fighter defined by the act of combat, distinct from kampjo (365, generic fighter/soldier) or from occupational warrior terms. Belongs to the same heroic register as gunþ (142) "battle" and wīg (998) "battle/fight."

Gothic þreis tigjus (still two words in Wulfila), OE þrītig, OHG drīzzug (post-second-sound-shift). Pre-shift Ripuarian preserves intact þ- initial and intact intervocalic -t- (no shift to -zz-). þē

/θeː/

the (masculine article)
OHGdërOEþē
used in
Sigifriþ, þe kuninges sunu ist, ferit in rīne.
Sigifrīþ, who is the king's son, travels on the Rhine.
Ik willju sehan swerd, þat sigifriþ gaƀ.
I want to see the sword that Sigifrīþ gave.
Ik weit þat sigifriþ ist aiþbrōþer mīn.
I know that Sigifrīþ is my oath-brother.
Fader sagida þat helm was gōd.
Father said the helmet was good.
Þō warþ þemō Balderes folon sīn fōt biwrenkid.
Then Balder's foal's foot was wrenched.
Þeuda uƀarfōr Rīn, þe fraus.
The people crossed the Rhine, which had frozen.
Strong article / demonstrative pronoun "the, that". PGmc *sa / *þat / *sō with th-generalization in the paradigm (nom.sg.masc *sa was replaced by *þē in WGmc by analogy with the oblique th- stem). Cells hold masc paradigm; full three-gender declension follows. MASC sg: nom þē, gen þes, dat þemō, acc þan, instr þiu. FEM sg: nom þiu, gen þerā, dat þerō, acc þea. NEUT sg: nom þat, gen þes (= masc), dat þemō (= masc), acc þat, instr þiu. PL (largely gender-syncretic): nom.pl.masc þē / nom.pl.fem þea / nom.pl.neut þiu. gen.pl þerō (all genders). dat.pl þēm (all genders). acc.pl.masc þē / acc.pl.fem þea / acc.pl.neut þiu. Ripuarian preserves initial þ (unshifted) contra OHG d- (der/des/demo/den) and OS th- convergence. Medial -mm- in dat.sg reduces to -m- with the -ō ending giving þemō (compare OS themu, OHG demo, OE þǣm). Neut nom/acc.sg þat preserves the unshifted t (OHG daz shows the second sound shift t→ts). Fem/neut nom.sg þiu preserves the diphthong iu (from PGmc *sijō / *þiō). Used both as definite article (weakly stressed, proclitic) and as demonstrative pronoun (fully stressed, standalone). Attested in sentence 57 as dat.sg.masc þemō in the possessor-dative construction "þemō Balderes folon" ("to Balder's foal").

Temporal demonstrative adverb "then, at that time". From PGmc *þō. Cognates: OHG dō/duo (with ō → uo diphthongization), OS thō, OE þā, Goth. þan. Ripuarian preserves *þ (no consonant shift to d) and *ō (no OHG-style diphthongization to uo). Attested in the reconstructed compound þō-þar "then-there" (Merseburg Charm 1: OHG duoder < *þō-þar with initial and medial *þ → d and unstressed *ā weakened to -er).
